name: Beth Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. What you tell me is confidential, including differences from your public answer. Could you describe a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 43, and I lead electrical work in homes and businesses. I have a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm one of the strongest fault finders in our small firm. Yesterday I found why a shop's shutter motor kept tripping a circuit, then helped two colleagues finish their checks before closing. I use AI every day for organising job notes and testing a parts list, but the measurements, rules and final checks stay with us.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life like around that responsibility?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a bakery, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn low pay for this trade, we have three weeks of expenses saved, and there are few similar employers nearby. Being good and being able to leave are different matters here. I like trying a useful tool early, but I judge it by the repair and the bill, not whether it makes me sound keen on the future.

say: I'd value a **useful note assistant** without requiring it to be a miracle.
I'd keep repairs and records inside the **paid day**, while asking for an ordinary wage discussion.
think: My **master electrician's licence** and skill keep work coming without raising the low wage or creating another nearby employer.
Our **three-week reserve** still leaves me worried about the mortgage even if the technology story stays quiet.
do: Cancel my **audiobook subscription** now and use its cost for ordinary bills.
Continue leading **repair work** and checking customer handover notes through the first plateau year.
feel: **Anxious** about household money, with some relief about familiar work continuing.
S0.quote: A master electrician's licence doesn't turn three weeks of money into a month.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** comes from low wages and a short reserve despite high practical skill and responsibility for colleagues.
She treats the **subscription cut** as modest bill relief and will request better pay without pretending another job is already available.

steps.text: Cancel the audiobook subscription and put its cost towards bills
Continue leading electrical repairs and checking customer handover notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful note assistant doesn't need to become a miracle. I'd still want us to finish the repair and the record inside the paid day. A quieter story might leave more room to discuss an ordinary wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the mortgage with only three weeks behind us. My licence and skill keep the work coming, but the wage is low and the next employer isn't waiting around the corner. A master electrician's licence doesn't turn three weeks of money into a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel my paid audiobook subscription and use its cost for the ordinary bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep leading the repair work and checking the notes before customer handover. I wouldn't call a small spending cut a new emergency fund while the bills still needed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with some relief that the work itself stays familiar. I'd still be checking the account before the mortgage payment. I can enjoy an easier job sheet without calling the household secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use instead of the subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use library recordings rather than ask the children to give up their regular school things first. It wouldn't replace a wage or make a repair bill harmless. I'd want to be honest about how small the change was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for higher pay in this quieter picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring examples of the faults I solved and the crew work I covered to the pay review. I wouldn't threaten to resign without another written offer. Keeping a roof over the children matters more than winning an argument in the yard.

say: I'd trial a tool against **wrong-part return visits**, not just applaud a faster list.
I'd ask what happens to **paid preparation** rather than let saved office time become unpaid evening work.
think: My **paid planning time** could shrink or become extra calls, even while practical repairs still need doing.
A **small wage loss** would matter with our mortgage and three-week reserve, despite daily confidence with AI.
do: Trial **AI parts matching** on five fittings only in paid time with normal wages and hours, checking every replacement's actual rating.
Keep the **audiobook subscription** cancelled to reduce household bills.
Apply for posted **electrical vacancies** further away if wages fall, checking travel before accepting any offer.
feel: **Anxious** about pay, while interested in a checked trial that addresses a real repair problem.
S1.quote: A convincing photograph isn't a specification.
fieldNote: Her **new tool learning** concerns a distinct parts-matching function, rather than tagging the daily note use she already described.
The **wage risk** comes through paid planning and allowances, while actual fittings and approved ratings still govern the electrical decision.

steps.text: Learn the parts matcher only during paid work with normal wages and hours retained
Keep the audiobook subscription cancelled to reduce household bills
Apply for posted electrical jobs further away if wages fall, checking travel before acceptance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should try a tool where a wrong part costs us a second visit. I'd also ask what happens to the paid preparation time if software makes the lists faster. I'd want fewer wasted trips, not the same work quietly moved into my evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is still practical, but my paid planning time could shrink or turn into more calls for the same wage. A small income loss would matter in this house. Being quick with an app doesn't make me quick at paying a bigger mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask to learn the firm's approved new AI parts-photo matcher on five returned fittings during paid time, with normal wages and hours retained. In the first year I'd check every suggested replacement against the actual part and required rating before ordering. I'd keep the subscription cancelled and record actual paid preparation hours each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, but interested in finding out whether the new matcher solved a real problem. I don't need to protect a bad parts list. I need useful changes to leave the household able to pay its bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the matcher suggested the wrong rated fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop using that suggestion and show the mismatch with the actual fitting. A convincing photograph isn't a specification. I'd still make the final choice from the proper measurements and approved information.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm cut paid preparation hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the proposed paid hours in writing and compare them with the present arrangement. If the change cut my wage, I'd start applying to posted electrical vacancies beyond our usual local search, checking travel first. I wouldn't confuse agreeing to a tool trial with agreeing to less pay.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 and ask about actual future paid work.
I wouldn't treat a **difficult repair** as permanent shelter when machines eventually do practical work too.
think: I expect a **large repair-wage loss** as the firm moves towards capable hands-on robots.
My partner's wage and our **short reserve** cannot automatically replace my mortgage contribution.
do: Cancel the **audiobook subscription** now and use its cost for ordinary bills.
Ask for a **free mortgage appointment** now using actual wage and loan figures, assuming no relief or support approval.
Seek **posted electrical roles** after 2028; leave only on signed pay covering bills after travel, with changed school pickups agreed.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected major wage loss, with sleepless sums despite practical applications and enquiries.
S2.quote: I wouldn't call an unaffordable offer a rescue just because it was an offer.
fieldNote: Her **alarm** follows an expected large personal wage loss and sleep disruption, while she retains enough control to enquire and apply.
The **offer conditions** protect written household affordability, travel and agreed school pickups; advice and support remain unapproved possibilities.

steps.text: Cancel the audiobook subscription and use its cost for ordinary bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew to keep thinking work in 2028 separate from the hands-on robots around 2031. I'd use the gap to ask about actual work and wages, not tell everyone a difficult shop repair was permanent shelter. We still need enough paid work when the machines can do the practical parts too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a large part of my paid repair work to go as the firm moved towards capable robots. My partner's bakery wage couldn't automatically replace mine, and our reserve wouldn't carry the mortgage far. I'd be awake trying to make a few weeks of money cover a much longer gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel the audiobook subscription and ask for a free mortgage appointment using both actual wages and the loan figures. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for posted electrical roles that used my existing master-level skills, leaving only for a signed offer that covered household bills after travel. I'd agree any changed school pickups with my partner before accepting a shift pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a big wage loss in that picture, not just a form changing. I can still ask and apply. That doesn't make the mortgage calculation leave my head at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the mortgage appointment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the lender could actually offer and check any support eligibility, without assuming a payment pause or award. I'd take the limits home as well as the possibilities. The children would hear that we were making a plan, not that a form had already solved the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the first offered job was too far away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present wage and widen the actual application search before committing to a journey. If the written pay after travel didn't cover the bills, or the school pickups couldn't be agreed, I'd keep looking. I wouldn't call an unaffordable offer a rescue just because it was an offer.

I'd keep **robots around 2034** in view as the same end point arriving later.
think: More time could show where my **existing skills** earned better money without a speculative qualification bill.
Today's **low wage and mortgage** still make a three-week reserve feel too short.

Apply now for **posted electrical work** using current skills, continuing after 2031 only if household income remains insecure.
Leave only for a signed offer with written pay and **guaranteed hours** covering bills after travel, with changed school pickups agreed.

S3.quote: A higher number on an advert isn't the money that reaches the kitchen table.
fieldNote: She retains **baseline cash anxiety** while recognising that the longer preparation helps her examine actual jobs before moving.
Her **skill boundary** remains honest despite high standing, while system-specific teaching enquiries don't become a course she has chosen or funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check a better job while we still have wages. I'd keep the 2034 robot date in view rather than tell the children the trade had become safe. The same end point later is still the same end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd have longer to find out where my present skills earned decent money. But today I'd still have a low wage, a mortgage and three weeks behind us. More time would help the search without fixing the household account tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the subscription cancelled and make applications to posted electrical jobs using my existing skills, rather than pay for another qualification on speculation. In the first year after 2031 I'd continue that search if our wage still failed to cover the household safely. I'd leave only for a signed offer covering bills after travel, with changed school pickups agreed with my partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with less pressure to grab a poor next step. I'd still want to keep the children fed while we worked the route out. I wouldn't turn being experienced into a reason not to admit the wage was a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a posted job worth accepting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare written pay, guaranteed hours and actual travel before accepting. If it failed the household calculation, I'd keep this wage and keep applying elsewhere. A higher number on an advert isn't the money that reaches the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on unfamiliar systems for the higher wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what system-specific instruction came with the job before taking responsibility for unfamiliar work. A master licence doesn't mean I know every installed system already. I haven't chosen an expensive new course just because I asked the question.

I'd seek **paid work** using my skills without directing the children's whole future from one card.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I couldn't assume retirement or older children would replace the household wage.
Today's **low pay and reserve** still worry me even with much more time to examine alternatives.
do: Keep the **audiobook subscription** cancelled to reduce household bills.
Apply for **posted electrical jobs** now; review real wages and jobs yearly, continuing after 2036 only if household income remains insecure.
Leave only for a signed offer with written pay and **guaranteed hours** covering bills after travel, with changed family duties agreed.
feel: **Anxious** about present money, with more hope about gradual improvement and no invented future income.
S4.quote: Being adaptable should mean checking the result, not claiming every change worked.
fieldNote: She avoids **future-income assumptions** from age or older children, while adjusting the family-duty check to what is actually needed later.
Her **annual review** tests wages and real job options, without treating a longer deadline as permission to ignore current household pressure.

steps.text: Keep the audiobook subscription cancelled to reduce household bills
Apply now for posted electrical roles; continue after 2036 if household wages remain insecure
Require signed written pay and guaranteed hours covering bills after travel before leaving
Agree changed family duties with my partner before accepting another shift pattern

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should let us choose in stages instead of buying the first comforting career story. I'd keep asking what actual paid work used my skills. I wouldn't ask the children to choose a whole life around one technology card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change in 2036 and around 56 when robots followed. I can't assume retirement or older children would replace the wage. Right now I'd still have the same low pay and short reserve, even with more room to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the subscription cancelled and apply for posted electrical jobs that used my existing skills. Each year I'd compare actual wages, bills and reachable work rather than buy a promise of safety. In the first year after 2036 I'd continue applications if the household wage was still insecure, leaving only for a signed offer with written pay and guaranteed hours covering bills after travel, and actual changed family duties agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the current account, but more hopeful about having time to improve the working arrangement. A decade could let me correct a poor choice without making the next one in a panic. It wouldn't add money to the present account by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would later family duties automatically disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check what care the household actually needed then, not assume the children being grown meant nobody needed help. We'd agree any changed family duties before accepting a different shift pattern. I wouldn't count the children's future earnings as our plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep the decade from becoming waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask yearly whether the wage and paid hours had improved the household position. If not, I'd keep using actual applications and the mortgage advice rather than wait for 2036. Being adaptable should mean checking the result, not claiming every change worked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large repair-wage loss before we could build a useful buffer. Honest written hours and wages, and mortgage advice using our actual figures, would help more than a promise about my talent. Being good at electrical work doesn't let me move the mortgage date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the person who looks adaptable can actually afford the next step. I enjoy trying a tool and I'm good at the trade, but I still need the travel, pay and school pickup to work together. A plan with those details missing isn't a plan our household can use.

headlineQuote: Being good at electrical work doesn't let me move the mortgage date.
portrait: **Beth, 43**, is a highly skilled electrical lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and low pay.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and three weeks of expenses saved near few alternative employers.
She uses **AI daily**, tries useful tools early and checks real costs instead of assuming technical skill gives financial freedom.
Fast change brings **alarm** over expected major wage loss; slower timelines support actual applications without losing household, travel or family-duty conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens a large repair-wage loss before the household can build a useful buffer.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **written hours and wages** would help compare actual paid work.
**Mortgage advice** using actual household figures would clarify options without relying on praise for her skill.
